title: Pricing, Costing & Profit Planning
subtitle: Work out what every item really costs, set prices that make a profit, and plan the sales and cash your business needs each month.
description: A practical, numbers-first course for women running small businesses in Nigeria. You will sort and total every cost, calculate full unit cost, contribution margin and break-even point, set retail and wholesale prices with markup or margin, plan a monthly profit target, prepare a profit and loss statement and a cash flow forecast, and put it all into a one-page profit plan for your own business.
outcomes: Sort business costs into direct and indirect, fixed and variable, and calculate full cost per unit including wastage and your own wage
Calculate contribution margin, break-even point in units and naira, and margin of safety
Set retail and wholesale prices using markup or margin without confusing the two
Work back from a monthly profit target to weekly and daily sales targets
Prepare a monthly profit and loss statement and a weekly cash flow forecast, and explain why profit and cash differ
Build and review a one-page costing and profit plan, including what-if tests and price change decisions
audience: Women who already sell a product or service (food, cosmetics, tailoring, beauty or trading) and want to know their true costs and make a reliable profit.

A smartphone calculator, or Google Sheets on a phone or computer

modules.title: Know Every Cost: The Foundations of Pricing and Profit
modules.overview: Before you can set a good price you must see every naira your business spends. This module explains revenue, cost and profit, sorts costs into direct and indirect, fixed and variable, and gets your records and money habits ready for the calculations that follow.

lessons.title: Price, cost and profit: why busy is not the same as profitable
objectives: Explain the difference between revenue, cost and profit in your own words
Calculate profit or loss on one batch of goods
Spot the common hidden costs that make a busy business lose money
Describe what this course will help you produce for your own business

blocks.text: Many women in business sell every day, their customers are happy, and yet at the end of the month there is no money to show for it. Usually the problem is not hard work. The problem is that the price was set by guessing, by copying the woman at the next stall, or by adding a little to the cost of ingredients only. This course teaches you to replace guessing with simple calculations that you can do with a pen, a notebook and the calculator on your phone.
Three words you will use in every lesson

items: **Revenue** (also called sales or turnover): all the money customers pay you. If you sell 40 bottles at ₦300 each, revenue is 40 x ₦300 = ₦12,000.
**Cost**: all the money the business spends to make and sell those goods, including things you pay for once a month, like rent and data.
**Profit**: what is left after all costs are taken away from revenue. Profit = Revenue minus Total cost. If the answer is negative, it is a loss.

blocks.text: Notice that profit is not the same as the money in your hand at the end of the day. Cash in hand includes money you will soon spend on the next bag of sugar, money a customer paid in advance, and sometimes money you borrowed. We will separate profit from cash properly in Module 3. For now, remember: **money in your purse is not automatically profit.**

blocks.title: Worked example: the zobo seller who was working for free
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sells zobo in 50cl bottles near a motor park in Enugu for ₦300 a bottle. One batch makes 40 bottles. Prices below are approximate and only for practice.
steps: She lists what one batch uses: zobo leaves ₦2,500, ginger, pineapple peel and cloves ₦3,000, sugar ₦2,000, 40 empty bottles at ₦60 each = ₦2,400, clean water and ice ₦1,100, cooking gas ₦1,000.
Cost per bottle = ₦12,000 divided by 40 = ₦300. That is exactly her selling price.
She also pays ₦1,500 in transport to carry the cooler to the park, so total cost for the batch = 12,000 + 1,500 = ₦13,500.
Revenue if all 40 bottles sell = 40 x ₦300 = ₦12,000. Profit = 12,000 minus 13,500 = minus ₦1,500.
blocks.result: Amaka loses about ₦1,500 on every batch, and she has not yet counted her own time. Selling more would only make the loss bigger. She needs a higher price, a cheaper way to make the drink, or both.

blocks.text: The costs people forget
When small business owners check their prices, these are the costs most often left out. Read the list and tick the ones that apply to you.

items: **Your own labour.** If you do not pay yourself, your price is too low. One day you will need to hire help, and the price must already carry that wage.
**Packaging and labels**: nylon, bottles, stickers, cartons, carrier bags.
**Transport**: trips to the market for supplies and trips to deliver orders.
**Energy**: gas, kerosene, charcoal, electricity bills, generator fuel.
**Phone data and airtime** used to take orders on WhatsApp and post on social media.
**Wastage**: burnt batches, broken items, unsold perishables.
**Equipment wear**: a fryer, sealer or sewing machine that will need replacing.
**Fees and levies**: market or association dues, POS and transfer charges, registration.

blocks.title: Copying a competitor's price is risky
blocks.text: The woman beside you may buy in bulk, use family labour, or be losing money without knowing it. Always know your own cost first. Then compare with the market to decide where to position your price.

blocks.title: From costs to a safe price
items: List every cost

blocks.caption: This course follows this order: costs first, then profit, then the market, then regular review.

blocks.text: What you will produce in this course

By the end you will have a one-page costing and profit plan for your real business: a full cost per unit, your break-even point (the number of sales at which you stop losing money), a monthly profit target with a plan to reach it, a simple monthly profit and loss statement, and a cash flow forecast. Each module adds one piece, and the final project puts them together.

blocks.title: Use one notebook
blocks.text: Buy one exercise book just for this course and your business numbers. Write the date on every page. A single notebook is easier to check than receipts scattered in bags and WhatsApp chats. If you prefer your phone, a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets works just as well; the calculations are the same.

takeaways: Profit = Revenue minus Total cost; a negative answer is a loss
Selling more at a loss-making price only makes the loss bigger
Your own labour, packaging, transport, energy, data and wastage are real costs
Know your own cost before you compare with a competitor's price

lessons.title: Direct and indirect costs, fixed and variable costs
objectives: Sort any business cost as direct or indirect
Sort any business cost as fixed or variable
Calculate total variable cost and total fixed cost for a month
Explain why mixed costs need to be split

blocks.text: To price well, you need to sort your costs in two different ways. Each way answers a different question. The first sorting asks: **can I trace this cost to one particular product?** The second asks: **does this cost go up and down when I make more or fewer items?** The same cost can be described both ways.
Direct and indirect costs

items: **Direct costs** can be traced to a single product or order. In tailoring, the lining, zip, buttons and thread used in one gown are direct costs of that gown.
**Indirect costs** (often called overheads) support the whole business and cannot be traced to one item. Shop rent, the apprentice's monthly stipend, generator fuel and phone data are indirect costs.

blocks.text: Fixed and variable costs

items: **Variable costs** rise and fall with how much you produce or sell. Make twice as many packs of chin-chin and you use about twice as much flour, oil and packaging.
**Fixed costs** stay about the same each month whether you sell a little or a lot, at least within your normal range of work. Rent, your own monthly wage, and a market levy are fixed costs.

**Mixed (semi-variable) costs** have a fixed part and a variable part. A generator may run every working day to light the shop (fixed part) and run longer in busy weeks (variable part). Estimate the two parts separately when you can.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting Halima's tailoring costs for one month
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs a small tailoring shop in Kaduna. Customers bring their own fabric; she supplies lining and accessories. In a normal month she sews about 40 garments. Prices are approximate.
steps: Direct materials for one gown: lining 2 yards at ₦1,500 = ₦3,000, zip ₦300, thread ₦200, interfacing ₦500, buttons ₦400. Total = 3,000 + 300 + 200 + 500 + 400 = ₦4,400 per gown.
These materials are direct and variable: 40 gowns x ₦4,400 = ₦176,000 a month if every garment were a gown like this.
Monthly indirect costs: rent ₦30,000, apprentice ₦20,000, generator fuel ₦24,000, phone data ₦6,000. Total = 30,000 + 20,000 + 24,000 + 6,000 = ₦80,000.
She treats these indirect costs as fixed, because they barely change between a quiet month and a busy month.
Indirect cost carried by each garment in a 40-garment month = ₦80,000 divided by 40 = ₦2,000.
blocks.result: Each gown carries ₦4,400 of direct materials plus ₦2,000 share of overheads, so ₦6,400 before Halima pays herself or makes any profit. If she charged ₦6,000 for sewing, she would be losing money on every gown.

blocks.text: Why the overhead share changes with volume

Look again at the ₦80,000 of fixed costs. In a slow month with only 20 garments, each garment must carry ₦80,000 divided by 20 = ₦4,000 of overhead. In a busy month of 50 garments, each carries ₦80,000 divided by 50 = ₦1,600. The variable cost per gown stays ₦4,400 either way. This is why busy months feel profitable and slow months hurt so much: **fixed costs do not shrink when sales fall.**

blocks.title: Equipment is a cost even after you have paid for it
blocks.text: A sealing machine bought for ₦72,000 that will last about 24 months costs the business roughly ₦72,000 divided by 24 = ₦3,000 a month. Accountants call this depreciation. Include it as a fixed cost so that your prices save up for the replacement.
A quick test for any cost

items: Ask: if I made no items at all this month, would I still pay this? If yes, it is fixed (or the fixed part of a mixed cost).
Ask: if I made double the items, would this cost roughly double? If yes, it is variable.
Ask: can I say exactly how much of this went into one item? If yes, it is direct; if not, it is indirect.
Write the answer beside each cost in your notebook.

blocks.title: Keep the business wage separate
blocks.text: Write your own monthly wage as a fixed cost, even if you only take it when sales are good. A price that does not cover your wage is subsidised by your unpaid time. If family members help without pay, estimate what you would pay a helper for those hours too, so the price still works on the day you hire someone.

takeaways: Direct costs trace to one product; indirect costs (overheads) support the whole business
Variable costs move with output; fixed costs stay about the same each month
Fixed cost per item falls when you sell more and rises when you sell less
Equipment wear and your own wage belong in fixed costs

lessons.title: Getting ready: honest records, separate money and safe payments
objectives: Set up a simple record system that captures every cost
Separate business money from household money
Measure real quantities instead of guessing them
Protect your business from payment scams and customer data leaks

blocks.text: Every calculation in this course is only as good as the numbers you put in. If your flour price is three months old, or you guess that a bag of sugar makes 'about ten batches' without checking, your price will be wrong. This lesson prepares the ground: records, measurements, a separate business account, and protection against the scams that target traders who receive transfers.
1. Capture every cost for at least two weeks

items: Keep every receipt in one envelope or snap a photo of it into a WhatsApp chat with yourself named 'Business costs'.
When there is no receipt (market purchases, okada fares), write the amount in your notebook the same day.
Note the quantity as well as the price: '10 kg flour, ₦15,000', not just '₦15,000'.
At the end of each week, copy the totals into your cost table from Lesson 1.2.

blocks.text: 2. Measure, do not guess

Weigh a whole batch the first time you cost it. A kitchen scale that reads in grams is one of the best investments a food or cosmetics business can make. Count how many good units a batch really gives, after removing burnt, broken or misshapen ones. If a 50 kg bag of flour gives you exactly five 10 kg batches, write that down; do not rely on what the seller told you.

blocks.name: receipt
blocks.alt: A person checking a long receipt
blocks.caption: A receipt with quantity and price is the raw material for every cost calculation.

blocks.title: Worked example: turning a week of receipts into costs
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi fries and packs chin-chin in Owerri. She collected her receipts for one week in which she made 4 batches of 50 packs. Prices are approximate.
steps: Flour: two purchases of 10 kg at ₦15,000 and one 20 kg purchase at ₦30,000. Total flour = 40 kg for ₦60,000, which is ₦15,000 per 10 kg batch.
Vegetable oil: 20 litres bought for ₦40,000, used across the 4 batches, so ₦10,000 per batch.
Packaging: 200 printed pouches at ₦80 each = ₦16,000, so ₦4,000 per batch of 50.
She checks: 4 batches x 50 packs = 200 packs made. She found 6 broken or burnt packs, so she sold 194 good packs.
She writes all of this into her notebook with dates, and notes that wastage was 6 out of 200, which is 3 percent.
blocks.result: Ngozi now has real, dated costs per batch for her three biggest items and a measured wastage rate of 3 percent, ready for the unit cost calculation in Module 2.

blocks.text: 3. Separate business money from household money

When sales money and housekeeping money sit in one purse or one account, you cannot tell whether the business is making profit. Open a separate account or wallet for the business. Many Nigerian banks and mobile money providers such as OPay and Moniepoint offer accounts you can open from your phone. Pay all business costs from it, receive all sales into it, and pay yourself a fixed wage from it into your personal account.

blocks.text: 4. Protect your money from payment scams

items: **Fake credit alerts**: some fraudsters show a fake transfer screenshot or send an SMS that looks like a bank alert. Confirm every payment inside your bank or wallet app, or on your POS, before releasing goods.
**OTP and PIN requests**: no genuine bank, POS company or customer needs your PIN, password or one-time code. Never share them, even with someone claiming to be bank staff.
**Overpayment tricks**: a 'customer' sends too much and asks you to refund the extra. Wait until the full amount shows in your app and check it is not reversed.
**Supplier account changes**: if a supplier suddenly sends new account details, call them on the number you already have before paying.

blocks.title: Customer data is your responsibility
blocks.text: Customer phone numbers, addresses and payment details should be used only for their orders. Do not post order screenshots that show other people's numbers or addresses. Nigeria has a Nigeria Data Protection Act (2023), so treat personal data with care: share it only when needed and delete what you no longer need.
5. Decide your own wage now

Write a monthly amount you would accept to do this work for someone else. This is not a dream number; it is a fair wage for your hours. You will include it as a fixed cost in every calculation. If the business cannot yet pay it, the calculations will show you how many more sales or how much higher a price you need, which is far better than hiding the gap. Review the wage once a year, or sooner if prices in the market rise sharply.

takeaways: Wrong or old numbers give wrong prices, so capture costs with dates and quantities
Weigh and count real batches, and measure wastage
Keep business money in a separate account and pay yourself a fixed wage
Confirm every payment in your app and never share your PIN or OTP

A dispatch rider for one order

quiz.q: Halima's fixed costs are ₦80,000 a month. In a slow month she sews only 20 garments. How much overhead must each garment carry?

Ask the customer for her OTP to check

modules.title: Guided Practice: Unit Cost, Break-Even and Setting Your Price
modules.overview: Now you put the numbers to work. You will calculate the full cost of one unit, find the contribution each sale makes and the break-even point, and then set retail and wholesale prices using markup or margin without the common mistakes.

lessons.title: Calculating unit cost step by step
objectives: Cost a full batch line by line and find the variable cost per unit
Share monthly fixed costs across your expected sales
Calculate full cost per unit
Adjust unit cost for wastage

blocks.text: Unit cost is what it costs you to produce and sell **one** item: one pack, one bottle, one gown, one hairdo. It has two parts. The **variable cost per unit** comes from the batch or job itself. The **fixed cost per unit** is your share of monthly overheads, spread across the number of units you expect to sell in a month. Add them and you have the **full cost per unit**, the lowest price at which you cover everything, including your own wage.
The four-step method

items: List every variable cost for one batch, with quantity and price.
Add them and divide by the number of good units the batch gives. This is variable cost per unit.
Add up all monthly fixed costs and divide by the number of units you realistically sell in a month. This is fixed cost per unit.
Add the two: full cost per unit = variable cost per unit + fixed cost per unit.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's full cost per pack
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi (from Lesson 1.3) makes chin-chin in 250 g packs. One batch gives 50 good packs. She expects to sell about 200 packs a month.
steps: Variable cost per pack = ₦47,000 divided by 50 = ₦940.
Monthly fixed costs: share of kitchen rent ₦25,000, her own wage ₦60,000, phone data ₦8,000, market levy ₦3,000, equipment wear ₦3,000, supply trips ₦11,000. Total = ₦110,000.
Fixed cost per pack at 200 packs a month = ₦110,000 divided by 200 = ₦550.
Full cost per pack = ₦940 + ₦550 = ₦1,490.
blocks.result: At 200 packs a month each pack really costs Ngozi about ₦1,490. Her old price of ₦1,500 leaves only ₦10 of profit per pack, so she is close to working for her wage alone with nothing left to grow the business.

blocks.text: Step 3: choose a realistic monthly volume

The fixed cost per unit depends on the volume you divide by, so be honest. Use your average sales over the last two or three months, not your best month. If Ngozi used her best-ever month of 300 packs, she would get ₦110,000 divided by 300 = about ₦367 per pack, a full cost of about ₦1,307, and she would believe she is more profitable than she is. If you are just starting, use a careful estimate and recheck after the first month.
Adjusting for wastage

Burnt, broken or unsold items are not free. Their cost must be carried by the good units. The rule is simple: **divide the batch cost by the number of good units, not the number you planned.** If one of Ngozi's batches gives only 48 good packs instead of 50, her variable cost per good pack becomes ₦47,000 divided by 48 = about ₦979, roughly ₦39 more per pack. Over 200 packs a month that is close to ₦8,000 of hidden cost. Reducing wastage is often the cheapest way to increase profit.

blocks.title: Cost from the price you will pay next time
blocks.text: When prices are rising, use the price you will pay for your next purchase, not what you paid two months ago. Call or message your supplier before you recalculate. Write the date beside every price, and keep the old price too so you can see how fast costs are moving.
Unit cost for a service

If you sell a service, such as hair braiding, make-up or lessons, the 'unit' is one job or one hour. Variable costs are the materials used on that job (attachment hair, gel, products) plus any helper paid per job. Fixed costs per job are your monthly overheads divided by the number of jobs you do in a typical month. Your time is usually the biggest cost, so make sure your wage is in the fixed costs.

blocks.title: Rounding
blocks.text: Work in whole naira and round unit costs up, not down. Rounding up protects your profit; rounding down quietly gives it away.

takeaways: Full cost per unit = variable cost per unit + fixed cost per unit
Divide batch cost by good units, so wastage is included
Spread fixed costs over a realistic, average monthly volume
Use current prices with dates, and round unit costs up

lessons.title: Contribution margin and your break-even point
objectives: Calculate contribution margin per unit and contribution margin ratio
Calculate break-even point in units and in naira
Calculate margin of safety
Use break-even to compare two possible prices

blocks.text: Full cost per unit is useful, but it changes every time your sales volume changes. Break-even analysis gives you a steadier way to think. It answers the question every business owner asks: **how many do I need to sell each month before I start making money?**
Contribution margin

Each sale brings in the selling price. Part of that money immediately pays for the variable cost of the item. What is left over is the **contribution margin**: it contributes first to paying fixed costs, and once those are covered, it becomes profit.

items: **Contribution margin per unit** = Selling price minus Variable cost per unit.
**Contribution margin ratio** = Contribution margin per unit divided by Selling price. It tells you how many kobo of every naira of sales are left to cover fixed costs and profit.
**Break-even point in units** = Total monthly fixed costs divided by Contribution margin per unit. Always round **up** to the next whole unit.
**Break-even sales in naira** = Break-even units x Selling price (or Fixed costs divided by Contribution margin ratio).

blocks.title: Finding break-even
items: Selling price
Minus variable cost
Equals contribution per unit
Fixed costs divided by contribution
Break-even units
blocks.caption: Contribution per unit is the bridge between your price and the number of sales you need.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's break-even at ₦1,500 a pack
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's variable cost is ₦940 a pack and her fixed costs are ₦110,000 a month (from Lesson 2.1). She currently sells at ₦1,500.
steps: Contribution margin per pack = ₦1,500 minus ₦940 = ₦560.
Contribution margin ratio = 560 divided by 1,500 = 0.373, about 37 percent.
Break-even units = ₦110,000 divided by ₦560 = 196.4. Round up: 197 packs.
Check: 197 x ₦560 = ₦110,320, which covers ₦110,000. At 196 packs she would have only ₦109,760, which is short.
Break-even sales in naira = 197 x ₦1,500 = ₦295,500.
blocks.result: Ngozi must sell 197 packs, about ₦295,500 of sales, every month just to cover her costs including her wage. Only the 198th pack onwards gives profit, ₦560 each.

blocks.text: Margin of safety

The **margin of safety** is how far your sales can fall before you hit break-even. Margin of safety = Expected sales minus Break-even sales. If Ngozi expects to sell 250 packs, her margin of safety is 250 minus 197 = 53 packs. As a percentage: 53 divided by 250 = about 21 percent. A thin margin of safety, below about 10 percent, means one bad week could push the month into a loss.
Using break-even to test a new price

Suppose Ngozi raises her price to ₦1,700. Her variable cost stays ₦940, so contribution becomes ₦1,700 minus ₦940 = ₦760 a pack. Break-even = ₦110,000 divided by ₦760 = 144.7, rounded up to 145 packs (check: 145 x 760 = ₦110,200). A ₦200 price rise cuts the packs she needs to break even from 197 to 145, a drop of 52 packs a month. She must judge whether customers will accept ₦1,700; if most still buy, the business becomes much safer.

blocks.name: growth-chart
blocks.alt: A person beside a rising chart
blocks.caption: Above the break-even point, every extra sale adds its full contribution to profit.

blocks.title: Never sell below variable cost
blocks.text: If a price is lower than the variable cost, each sale loses money before rent or wages are even considered. For Ngozi, any price under ₦940 makes every extra pack a direct loss. Clearance of stock about to spoil is the only usual exception.

blocks.title: Worked example: break-even for a braiding service
blocks.context: For example, Zainab braids knotless braids from a rented chair in a salon in Abuja and charges ₦12,000 per head. Prices are approximate.
steps: Variable cost per head: attachment hair ₦3,500, gel and mousse ₦500, assistant paid ₦1,000 per head. Total = ₦5,000.
Contribution per head = ₦12,000 minus ₦5,000 = ₦7,000.
Monthly fixed costs: chair rent ₦20,000, her own wage ₦50,000, data ₦5,000, share of power ₦15,000. Total = ₦90,000.
Break-even = ₦90,000 divided by ₦7,000 = 12.9, rounded up to 13 heads. Check: 13 x 7,000 = ₦91,000.
blocks.result: Zainab needs 13 clients a month, roughly three a week, to cover all costs including her wage. Every client after that adds ₦7,000 of profit.

blocks.text: What break-even assumes

The calculation assumes one price, one variable cost and that everything you make is sold. Real life is messier. If you sell several products, work out break-even for your main product first, or use an average contribution per sale from your records. If you discount often, use your average actual selling price, not the price on the label.

blocks.title: Turn monthly targets into daily ones
blocks.text: If you sell 26 days a month, 197 packs is about 197 divided by 26 = 7.6, so 8 packs a day. Daily targets are easier to track on a stall.

takeaways: Contribution margin per unit = price minus variable cost
Break-even units = fixed costs divided by contribution per unit, rounded up
Margin of safety shows how much sales can fall before a loss
A small price rise can cut the break-even point sharply

activity.title: Find your break-even point
steps: Write your selling price and variable cost per unit from Lesson 2.1.
Calculate contribution margin per unit and the contribution margin ratio.
Divide your monthly fixed costs by the contribution per unit and round up.
Compare break-even with your average monthly sales and calculate your margin of safety.
Repeat the calculation for a price ₦100 or ₦200 higher and note the difference.
activity.evidence: A worked page showing contribution margin, break-even units and naira, margin of safety, and the comparison at a higher price

lessons.title: Setting retail and wholesale prices without the common mistakes
objectives: Explain the difference between markup and margin
Calculate a price that delivers a target margin
Set a wholesale price that still contributes to fixed costs
Find and correct common pricing errors

blocks.text: You now know your full cost and your break-even point. The next step is choosing a selling price. Most small businesses use **cost-plus pricing**: start from cost and add a profit. There are two ways to add it, and confusing them is one of the most common and costly mistakes in small business.
Markup and margin are not the same

items: **Markup** is profit as a percentage of **cost**. Price = Cost x (1 + markup). A ₦1,000 item with 50 percent markup sells for ₦1,500.
**Margin** is profit as a percentage of **selling price**. Price = Cost divided by (1 minus margin). A ₦1,000 item with 50 percent margin sells for ₦1,000 divided by 0.5 = ₦2,000.
The same ₦500 profit on a ₦1,500 price is a 50 percent markup but only a 33 percent margin (500 divided by 1,500).

blocks.title: Markup versus margin
items: Markup
Margin
blocks.caption: For the same percentage, a margin target always gives a higher price than a markup target.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi tests markup and margin prices
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's full cost at 200 packs a month is ₦1,490 a pack (Lesson 2.1). She wants to see what a 30 percent target would mean.
steps: 30 percent markup: ₦1,490 x 1.30 = ₦1,937.
Check the margin this gives: profit ₦1,937 minus ₦1,490 = ₦447; 447 divided by 1,937 = about 23 percent margin, not 30.
30 percent margin: ₦1,490 divided by 0.70 = ₦2,128.57, round up to ₦2,130.
Check: profit ₦2,130 minus ₦1,490 = ₦640; 640 divided by 2,130 = about 30 percent. Correct.
She checks the market: similar 250 g packs in her area sell, for example, between about ₦1,500 and ₦2,000. ₦2,130 is above that range.
blocks.result: Ngozi chooses ₦1,700 for now, which customers accept, and plans to raise volume so that her fixed cost per pack falls. Cost-plus told her the price she would like; the market told her the price she can get today. She needs both.

blocks.text: Two other ways to think about price

items: **Competitor-based pricing**: you set your price near what similar sellers charge. It is quick, but only safe if your own cost is lower than that price.

**Value-based pricing**: you price by what the product is worth to the customer, for example a cake for a wedding, a rush tailoring job or delivery to the office. Customers often pay more for speed, reliability, quality and convenience. Your cost is still the floor.

blocks.text: Setting a wholesale price

Shops, supermarkets and resellers buy in bulk and must make their own profit, so they need a lower price than your retail customers. A wholesale price must still be **above your variable cost** and should make a real contribution. If Ngozi sells to a provisions shop at ₦1,400 a pack, her contribution per pack is ₦1,400 minus ₦940 = ₦460, and the shop can resell at ₦1,700 and keep ₦300. Set a minimum order, for example 20 packs, so the lower price is earned by volume.

blocks.name: business-shop
blocks.alt: A small shop front with a shopkeeper
blocks.caption: Wholesale customers such as provisions shops need room for their own profit, so your price to them must be planned.

blocks.text: Common pricing mistakes and how to fix them

head: Mistake
Why it hurts
Fix
rows: Adding a markup when you meant a margin
Profit comes out lower than planned
Use Price = Cost divided by (1 minus margin)
Your time is unpaid and hiring help later is impossible
Put your wage in fixed costs
Rising costs eat your margin unnoticed
Recheck prices monthly and date them
Good units secretly carry the cost of bad ones
Keep wholesale above variable cost with a minimum order

blocks.title: Worked example: correcting a body butter price
blocks.context: For example, Funke makes whipped shea body butter in Ibadan. Her full cost per jar is ₦2,000. She wanted a 50 percent margin, so she priced at ₦3,000.
steps: Her actual margin: profit ₦3,000 minus ₦2,000 = ₦1,000; 1,000 divided by 3,000 = 33 percent. She used a 50 percent markup by mistake.
Correct price for a 50 percent margin: ₦2,000 divided by 0.5 = ₦4,000.
She checks local prices and decides ₦4,000 is too high for her market, so she settles on ₦3,500, a margin of ₦1,500 divided by ₦3,500 = about 43 percent.
blocks.result: Funke now knows exactly what margin she is earning and made a conscious choice, instead of believing she had 50 percent when she had 33.

blocks.title: Round to prices customers like
blocks.text: Round up to amounts that are easy to pay and give change for, such as ₦1,700 or ₦3,500. Avoid awkward amounts like ₦1,937.

takeaways: Markup is based on cost; margin is based on selling price
For a target margin, Price = Cost divided by (1 minus margin)
Wholesale prices must stay above variable cost and come with a minimum order
Cost-plus gives the price you need; the market tells you what you can charge today

activity.title: Price your product two ways
steps: Take your full cost per unit from Lesson 2.1.
Calculate the price for a 30 percent markup and for a 30 percent margin.
Check prices for similar products in two shops, stalls or online pages and write them down.
Choose a retail price and calculate the margin it gives you.
Set a wholesale price and minimum order, and check it is above your variable cost.
activity.evidence: A price sheet with markup and margin calculations, market prices seen, and your chosen retail and wholesale prices

quiz.q: A batch costs ₦47,000 and gives 48 good packs instead of the planned 50. What is the variable cost per good pack, to the nearest naira?
quiz.explain: Divide by good packs: ₦47,000 divided by 48 = ₦979.17, about ₦979. Wastage raises the cost of every good pack.

quiz.q: Ngozi's fixed costs are ₦110,000 a month. Her price is ₦1,700 and variable cost ₦940. What is her break-even point?
quiz.explain: Contribution = 1,700 minus 940 = ₦760. 110,000 divided by 760 = 144.7, rounded up to 145 packs.

quiz.q: An item costs ₦1,000 in full. Kemi wants a 40 percent margin. What price should she charge?
quiz.explain: Price = Cost divided by (1 minus margin) = 1,000 divided by 0.6 = ₦1,666.67, about ₦1,667. ₦1,400 would be a 40 percent markup, giving only about a 29 percent margin.

quiz.q: Ngozi expects to sell 250 packs and her break-even is 197 packs. What is her margin of safety?
quiz.explain: Margin of safety = 250 minus 197 = 53 packs. 53 divided by 250 = about 21 percent.

quiz.q: A supermarket asks Ngozi for 100 packs at ₦900 each. Her variable cost is ₦940. What should she do?
options: Accept, because big orders always help
Accept and make up the loss on retail sales
Decline or counter-offer above ₦940, because each pack would lose ₦40 before fixed costs
Accept only if they pay cash
quiz.explain: A price below variable cost loses money on every unit, here ₦40 a pack or ₦4,000 on the order, before any fixed costs. She should counter-offer a price above ₦940, ideally one with a real contribution such as ₦1,400.

modules.title: Profit Targets, Monthly Profit and Loss, and Cash Flow
modules.overview: This module turns your prices into a plan and a record. You will set a monthly profit target and work back to the sales you need, prepare a monthly profit and loss statement with the key numbers to watch, and learn why a profitable business can still run out of cash.

lessons.title: Setting a profit target and working back to the sales you need
objectives: Calculate the units needed to reach a monthly profit target
Break a monthly target into weekly and daily targets
Check a target against your production capacity
Compare the four levers that raise profit

blocks.text: Break-even tells you how to stop losing money. A **profit target** tells you how to make the money you actually want. The method is a small extension of the break-even formula: you simply add the profit you want to the fixed costs before dividing.

Choose a target based on what the profit must pay for, not a round number that sounds nice. Profit is the money that buys a new fryer or sewing machine, builds an emergency buffer, repays a loan, and lets the business grow. Your wage is already in fixed costs, so the target is money for the business itself. Start with a modest figure, reach it for two or three months, then raise it.

blocks.title: The formula
blocks.text: Units needed for target profit = (Monthly fixed costs + Target profit) divided by Contribution margin per unit. Round up to the next whole unit.

blocks.title: From profit target to daily sales
items: Choose monthly profit target
Add monthly fixed costs
Divide by contribution per unit
Units needed per month
Weekly and daily targets
blocks.caption: Working backwards from the profit you want turns a wish into a number you can track each day.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi wants ₦100,000 profit a month
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi now sells at ₦1,700 a pack. Variable cost is ₦940, so contribution is ₦760. Fixed costs are ₦110,000 a month, and her own ₦60,000 wage is already inside them. She wants ₦100,000 profit on top, to save for a bigger fryer.
steps: Fixed costs plus target profit = ₦110,000 + ₦100,000 = ₦210,000.
Packs needed = ₦210,000 divided by ₦760 = 276.3. Round up: 277 packs a month.
Check: 277 x ₦760 = ₦210,520, enough. 276 x ₦760 = ₦209,760, slightly short.
Sales value needed = 277 x ₦1,700 = ₦470,900 a month.
Weekly target = 277 divided by 4 = 69.25, so 70 packs a week. Over 26 selling days, 277 divided by 26 = 10.7, so 11 packs a day.
blocks.result: Ngozi's target becomes something she can track: 11 packs a day, 70 a week, 277 a month. She needs 6 batches a month (6 x 50 = 300 packs) to have enough stock.

blocks.text: Check the target against capacity

A target is only useful if you can produce and sell that much. Ask three questions. Can I make it? Ngozi can fry about two batches a week with one helper, so 6 to 8 batches a month is possible. Can I sell it? She sold about 250 packs last month, so 277 is a stretch of about 11 percent, not a fantasy. Can I fund it? Each batch costs ₦47,000 to make before any money comes back, so she needs working cash to start. We return to that in Lesson 3.3.
How price changes the target

At ₦1,500, Ngozi would have to make and sell 375 packs, about one and a half times her current sales, for the same profit she can earn from 277 packs at ₦1,700. Low prices demand far more work, more stock and more cash for the same reward.

blocks.name: target
blocks.alt: A person aiming at a target
blocks.caption: A clear monthly profit target, turned into daily sales, gives your work a direction you can measure.

blocks.text: The four profit levers

items: **Raise the price**: often the strongest lever, but test it with customers and give reasons, such as better packaging or reliable delivery.

**Cut variable cost**: buy in bulk, reduce wastage, negotiate with suppliers. For example, a 50 kg bag of flour at about ₦72,000 instead of five 10 kg bags at ₦15,000 (₦75,000) saves ₦3,000 every 5 batches, about ₦12 a pack.
**Cut fixed cost**: share a kitchen or stall, review data plans, drop costs that do not bring sales.
**Sell more units**: new outlets, wholesale customers, WhatsApp Status and repeat-customer offers.

blocks.title: Worked example: mixing retail and wholesale to reach the target
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi thinks she can sell 200 packs retail at ₦1,700 and wants to fill the rest of the target with wholesale at ₦1,400 (contribution ₦460).
steps: Retail contribution = 200 x ₦760 = ₦152,000.
Wholesale packs needed = ₦58,000 divided by ₦460 = 126.1, round up to 127 packs.
Total packs = 200 + 127 = 327, so she needs 7 batches (350 packs).
blocks.result: Wholesale helps volume, but because each wholesale pack contributes less, she needs 327 packs in total instead of 277. She decides to push retail first and use wholesale to clear extra stock.

blocks.title: Write the target where you see it
blocks.text: Write your daily target on the first page of your sales notebook and tick each day you reach it. At the end of each week, compare actual sales with the weekly target and adjust early.

takeaways: Units for target profit = (fixed costs + target profit) divided by contribution per unit
Turn a monthly target into weekly and daily numbers
Check every target against what you can make, sell and fund
Lower prices need far more volume for the same profit

activity.title: Set your own profit target
steps: Choose a realistic monthly profit you want on top of your wage.
Add it to your monthly fixed costs and divide by your contribution per unit; round up.
Turn the result into weekly and daily targets.
Check it against your production capacity and last month's sales.
Pick one profit lever you will use this month and write how.
activity.evidence: A target sheet showing the calculation, daily and weekly targets, capacity check and chosen lever

lessons.title: Your monthly profit and loss statement and the numbers to watch
objectives: Prepare a simple monthly profit and loss statement
Calculate gross profit, net profit, gross margin and net margin
Exclude unsold stock from the month's costs correctly
Compare actual results with your target

blocks.text: A **profit and loss statement** (P&L, also called an income statement) shows, for one period such as a month, what you sold, what it cost and what was left. It is the scorecard for everything you planned in the last lesson. You can prepare it in your notebook in about 30 minutes if your daily sales and costs are recorded.
The layout

items: **Sales (revenue)**: everything you sold in the month, including sales on credit that customers have not yet paid.
**Minus cost of goods sold**: the variable cost of the units you actually sold (not the ones still in stock).
**Equals gross profit.**
**Minus operating expenses**: your fixed costs, such as rent, your wage, data, levies and equipment wear.
**Equals net profit** (or net loss).

blocks.title: Profit and loss, top to bottom
items: Net profit
Minus operating expenses
Gross profit
Minus cost of goods sold
Sales
blocks.caption: Read a P&L from the bottom of this pyramid upwards: each line removes a layer of cost.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's P&L for one month
blocks.context: For example, in one month Ngozi made 7 batches (350 packs). She sold 260 packs retail at ₦1,700 and 60 packs to a supermarket at ₦1,400 on 30-day credit. 30 packs were still in stock at month end. Variable cost is ₦940 a pack.
steps: Retail sales = 260 x ₦1,700 = ₦442,000. Wholesale sales = 60 x ₦1,400 = ₦84,000. Total sales = ₦526,000.
Packs sold = 260 + 60 = 320. Cost of goods sold = 320 x ₦940 = ₦300,800. The 30 unsold packs (30 x ₦940 = ₦28,200) are stock, not this month's cost.
Operating expenses: rent ₦25,000, wage ₦60,000, data ₦8,000, levy ₦3,000, equipment wear ₦3,000, supply trips ₦11,000. Total ₦110,000.
blocks.result: Ngozi made a net profit of ₦115,200 after paying herself ₦60,000. That beats her ₦100,000 target by ₦15,200.

blocks.text: The key numbers to watch every month

items: **Gross margin** = Gross profit divided by Sales. For Ngozi: 225,200 divided by 526,000 = about 42.8 percent. If this falls, your input costs are rising or you are discounting too much.
**Net margin** = Net profit divided by Sales: 115,200 divided by 526,000 = about 21.9 percent. This is how many kobo of each naira you keep.
**Units sold against target**: 320 packs sold against a plan of 277.
**Stock at month end**: 30 packs worth ₦28,200 at cost. Rising unsold stock is an early warning.

blocks.name: ledger
blocks.caption: A monthly P&L written in the same ledger each month lets you compare months side by side.

blocks.title: Do not mix in personal spending
blocks.text: School fees, family contributions and household food are not business expenses. If you paid them from business money, record them as owner's drawings, separate from the P&L. Mixing them in hides whether the business itself is profitable.
Compare month by month

One P&L tells you little. Three in a row tell a story. Keep a simple table with months across the top and sales, gross profit, gross margin, net profit and net margin down the side. If sales rise but net margin falls, you may be selling more at too low a price, or costs may have climbed. If gross margin drops from about 43 percent to 38 percent while your price stayed the same, check what happened to flour, oil and packaging prices.
Break-even when you sell at more than one price

Ngozi sells at two prices, so her break-even from Lesson 2.2 no longer fits exactly. Use the P&L instead. Her average contribution per pack = gross profit divided by packs sold = ₦225,200 divided by 320 = about ₦704. Break-even = ₦110,000 divided by ₦704 = 156.3, rounded up to 157 packs. She sold 320, so her margin of safety is 320 minus 157 = 163 packs, about 51 percent of sales. That is a comfortable cushion.

Keep every monthly P&L. When you apply for a loan, a grant or a supplier's credit account, a lender will usually want to see records of your sales and profit. Twelve neat monthly statements in one notebook or spreadsheet show that you understand your business.

blocks.title: Record sales daily
blocks.text: Write every sale the day it happens: retail, wholesale and credit separately. POS and bank app histories from providers such as Moniepoint or OPay help, but cash sales must be written by hand. A P&L built from memory at month end is always wrong.

takeaways: Sales minus cost of goods sold = gross profit; minus operating expenses = net profit
Count only the variable cost of units sold; unsold units are stock
Watch gross margin, net margin, units against target and stock every month
Keep personal spending out of the P&L as owner's drawings

activity.title: Prepare last month's P&L
steps: Total last month's sales from your records, separating cash and credit sales.
Count units sold and multiply by your variable cost per unit to get cost of goods sold.
List and total your operating expenses for the month.
Calculate gross profit, net profit, gross margin and net margin.
Compare net profit with your target from Lesson 3.1 and write one reason for the difference.
activity.evidence: Your one-page monthly P&L with margins and a one-line comparison with your target

lessons.title: Cash flow versus profit: staying liquid and controlling money risks
objectives: Explain why profit and cash are different
Reconcile a month's profit to the change in cash
Prepare a simple cash flow forecast
Apply honest pricing practices and basic credit and fraud controls

blocks.text: Profit is a measure of whether the business is earning more than it spends over a period. **Cash flow** is the actual movement of money in and out of your account or purse. A business can show a healthy profit and still be unable to buy flour on Monday. Many small businesses fail not because they are unprofitable, but because they run out of cash.
Why profit and cash differ

items: **Credit sales**: counted as sales in the P&L, but no cash arrives until the customer pays.
**Unsold stock**: you paid cash to make it, but it is not yet a cost in the P&L.
**Equipment wear (depreciation)**: a cost in the P&L, but no cash leaves this month.
**Loan repayments**: cash leaves, but repaying the loan amount is not an expense in the P&L (interest is).
**Advance payments and deposits**: cash arrives before the sale is completed.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi's profit was ₦115,200, so where is the cash?
blocks.context: For example, take Ngozi's month from Lesson 3.2. She started with ₦40,000 in her business account. She also repaid ₦30,000 of a loan during the month.
steps: Cash in: retail sales ₦442,000. The supermarket's ₦84,000 is not due until next month. Cash in = ₦442,000.
Cash out: 7 batches made at ₦47,000 each = ₦329,000. Fixed costs paid in cash = ₦110,000 minus ₦3,000 equipment wear = ₦107,000. Loan repayment ₦30,000. Cash out = ₦466,000.
Net cash flow = ₦442,000 minus ₦466,000 = minus ₦24,000. Closing cash = ₦40,000 minus ₦24,000 = ₦16,000.
Reconcile: profit ₦115,200 + equipment wear ₦3,000 minus unpaid credit sale ₦84,000 minus unsold stock ₦28,200 minus loan repayment ₦30,000 = minus ₦24,000. It matches.
blocks.result: Ngozi earned ₦115,200 profit, yet her cash fell to ₦16,000, not enough to pay for even one ₦47,000 batch. Until the supermarket pays, she cannot keep production going without help.

blocks.title: The cash cycle
items: Cash
Buy materials
Produce stock
Sell
Collect payment
blocks.caption: Cash is locked up from the moment you buy materials until the customer pays; the longer the cycle, the more cash you need.

blocks.text: A simple cash flow forecast

A forecast lists, week by week, the cash you expect in and out. Start with opening cash, add expected receipts, subtract expected payments, and get closing cash, which becomes next week's opening cash. Any week that ends negative is a warning to act now: collect a debt, ask for a deposit, delay a purchase or produce less.

In this forecast, retail sales are 65 packs a week at ₦1,700 = ₦110,500. Fixed cash costs total ₦107,000 for the month (₦52,000 + ₦8,400 + ₦13,400 + ₦33,200), paid when they fall due. Collecting the supermarket's ₦84,000 in week 1 is what keeps week 1 positive. If that payment were late, week 1 would end at ₦16,000 + ₦110,500 minus ₦94,000 minus ₦52,000 = minus ₦19,500.

blocks.name: money-with-wings
blocks.caption: Cash can fly out of a profitable business through credit sales, stock and loan repayments.

blocks.text: Controlling credit and money risks

items: Take a deposit, for example 50 percent, before starting custom orders such as cakes, outfits or event packs.
Give credit only to known customers, write the amount and due date, and send a polite WhatsApp reminder on the due date.
Keep a cash buffer, ideally at least one month of fixed costs, before taking big credit orders.
Do not borrow to cover a business that is losing money; fix the price or costs first.
Be wary of 'investment' offers that promise high monthly returns with little risk; schemes like this have collapsed and taken traders' savings.

blocks.text: Ways to speed up your cash

items: Agree shorter payment terms with wholesale buyers, for example 14 days instead of 30, or a small discount for paying on delivery.
Buy perishable materials close to production day rather than weeks ahead.
Produce to match sales, so less cash sits in unsold stock.
Clear slow-moving stock early, at a price still above variable cost.

blocks.title: Honest pricing builds repeat customers
blocks.text: Make sure a pack labelled 250 g holds at least 250 g, display your prices clearly, honour prices you have quoted, and never advertise a 'was' price you never charged. When costs force a rise, tell customers plainly. Trust is worth more than one sale.

takeaways: Profit and cash differ because of credit sales, stock, depreciation, loans and deposits
Reconcile profit to cash change so you understand where money went
Forecast cash weekly and act early on any negative week
Use deposits, written credit terms, a cash buffer and honest pricing to control risk

activity.title: Build a four-week cash forecast
steps: Write your current business cash balance as week 1 opening cash.
List expected cash sales and debts to be collected for each of the next four weeks.
List expected payments: materials, fixed costs on their due dates, loan repayments.
Calculate closing cash for each week and carry it forward.
Mark any week that goes negative and write the action you will take.
activity.evidence: A four-week cash forecast table with any negative weeks marked and your planned actions

quiz.q: Ngozi's fixed costs are ₦110,000 and her contribution is ₦760 a pack. How many packs must she sell to make ₦100,000 profit?
quiz.explain: (110,000 + 100,000) divided by 760 = 276.3, rounded up to 277 packs. 145 is only the break-even point.

quiz.q: In one month a business has sales of ₦400,000, cost of goods sold of ₦240,000 and operating expenses of ₦100,000. What is the net margin?
quiz.explain: Gross profit = 400,000 minus 240,000 = ₦160,000. Net profit = 160,000 minus 100,000 = ₦60,000. Net margin = 60,000 divided by 400,000 = 15 percent. 40 percent is the gross margin.

quiz.q: Ngozi made 350 packs but sold 320. Her variable cost is ₦940. What is her cost of goods sold for the month?
quiz.explain: Only units sold count: 320 x ₦940 = ₦300,800. The 30 unsold packs are stock.

quiz.q: Ngozi's P&L shows ₦115,200 profit but her cash fell. Which of these is a reason?
options: A customer bought on credit and has not yet paid
Her wage is a fixed cost
quiz.explain: Credit sales count as sales in the P&L, but the cash only arrives when the customer pays. Equipment wear actually reduces profit without using cash.

quiz.q: A customer orders 40 packs of chin-chin for a wedding, to be collected in two weeks. What is the best way to protect Ngozi's cash?
options: Make the order and collect all payment on delivery
Ask for a deposit, for example 50 percent, before buying materials
Offer a large discount to win the order
Borrow money to make the order
quiz.explain: A deposit covers the materials, reduces the risk of a cancelled order and keeps her cash cycle healthy.

modules.title: Your Complete Costing and Profit Plan
modules.overview: In this final module you bring everything together into one costing and profit plan for your real business, learn to explain your prices and price changes to customers with confidence, and set up a monthly review routine that keeps your prices and profit healthy after the course ends.

lessons.title: Building your complete costing and profit plan
objectives: Assemble cost, break-even, target, P&L and cash figures into one plan
Check that every number in the plan agrees with the others
Write a short action plan with weekly targets
Present the plan on one page

blocks.text: You have now calculated each part of a profit plan separately. A plan is useful only when the parts agree with each other and fit on one page that you can look at every week. This lesson shows a complete plan for a service business, so you can see the method working outside food production, and then guides you to build your own.

blocks.title: The one-page profit plan
items: Cost table and unit cost
Price and contribution
Break-even point
Profit target and weekly sales
Projected P&L and cash notes
blocks.caption: Five sections, each built from a lesson in this course, make up your capstone plan.

blocks.text: Worked plan: Halima's tailoring shop

For example, Halima from Lesson 1.2 has updated her numbers. Her fixed costs of ₦80,000 now also include machine maintenance of ₦5,000 a month and her own wage of ₦70,000. Her 40 garments a month include many small repair jobs, so to be careful she plans on gowns only. Prices are approximate.

blocks.title: Worked example: Halima's costing and profit plan
blocks.context: Halima charges ₦15,000 to sew a gown; the customer brings the fabric and Halima supplies lining and accessories. She and her apprentice can sew about 8 gowns a week, so about 32 a month.
steps: Fixed costs: rent ₦30,000 + apprentice ₦20,000 + generator fuel ₦24,000 + data ₦6,000 + maintenance ₦5,000 + own wage ₦70,000 = ₦155,000 a month.
Variable cost per gown (lining, zip, thread, interfacing, buttons) = ₦4,400. Contribution = ₦15,000 minus ₦4,400 = ₦10,600.
Break-even = ₦155,000 divided by ₦10,600 = 14.6, rounded up to 15 gowns a month.
Profit target ₦80,000: (₦155,000 + ₦80,000) divided by ₦10,600 = 22.2, rounded up to 23 gowns a month, about 6 a week.
Plan volume 25 gowns: full cost per gown = ₦4,400 + (₦155,000 divided by 25 = ₦6,200) = ₦10,600, leaving ₦4,400 profit per gown at ₦15,000.
blocks.result: Halima needs 15 gowns to break even and 23 to hit her target. Her plan of 25 gowns sits well within her capacity of about 32 and gives a margin of safety of 10 gowns, 40 percent of planned sales.

head: Halima's projected monthly P&L at 25 gowns

blocks.text: Cash notes for the plan

Halima asks for a 50 percent deposit, ₦7,500, when a customer orders, and the balance at collection. Because the deposit is larger than the ₦4,400 she spends on materials for that gown, she never has to fund materials from her own pocket. Her biggest cash risk is the generator fuel, ₦24,000 a month, which she pays weekly. She keeps at least one month of fixed costs, ₦155,000, as a target cash buffer and is building towards it.

blocks.name: business-plan
blocks.alt: A person reviewing a business plan board
blocks.caption: A one-page plan puts your costs, break-even, target and cash notes where you can review them every week.

blocks.text: Checks before you call the plan finished

items: Every fixed cost appears once, including your wage and equipment wear.
The variable cost per unit in the break-even matches the one in your cost table.
Break-even and target are rounded up, and both are below your capacity.
The projected P&L uses the same price, variable cost and fixed costs.
Your cash notes say how you will fund materials before customers pay.
All prices are dated and marked as estimates where you are unsure.

blocks.text: Common gaps in first plans

items: Fixed costs listed without the owner's wage, so the plan looks profitable when it is not.
A volume taken from the best month ever instead of an average month.
A break-even point above what the business can actually produce in a month.
No plan for the cash needed before the first customers pay.
Old supplier prices with no dates beside them.

blocks.text: If you sell several products, build the plan around your two or three best sellers. Calculate contribution for each, then use your expected sales mix to find an average contribution per sale, as Ngozi did with retail and wholesale in Lesson 3.2. Keep small, occasional products out of the plan until they sell regularly.

blocks.title: Use a spreadsheet if you can
blocks.text: In Google Sheets, put price, variable cost and fixed costs in cells, then use formulas such as contribution = price minus variable cost and break-even = ROUNDUP(fixed costs / contribution, 0). When a cost changes, the whole plan updates at once.

blocks.title: Your capstone
blocks.text: The plan you build in this lesson is the core of your capstone project. Use real numbers from your business, not the examples. If a figure is an estimate, label it as an estimate and note how you will check it.

takeaways: A good plan fits on one page and every number agrees with the others
Break-even and profit targets must sit below your real capacity
Deposits that cover materials protect your cash
Label estimates honestly and update them as real numbers arrive

lessons.title: Explaining your price, handling discounts and raising prices
objectives: Describe the value behind your price in customer-friendly words
Calculate how many extra sales a discount requires
Recalculate a price when costs rise
Write a clear, polite price change message

blocks.text: Knowing your numbers gives you confidence, but customers do not buy numbers. They buy quality, freshness, reliability and convenience. This lesson shows you how to talk about value, why discounts are expensive, and how to raise a price when costs go up without losing your loyal customers.
Talk about value, not cost

items: Name the benefit: 'fried fresh every Tuesday and Friday', 'sealed pack, stays crunchy for weeks', 'full 250 g, weighed on a scale'.
Show proof: photos of your clean kitchen or workshop, a short video on WhatsApp Status, reviews from real customers who agree to be quoted.
Explain what is included: delivery within your area, fittings, adjustments, gift packaging.
Never apologise for your price. Say it clearly and wait.

blocks.text: The real cost of a discount

A discount comes straight out of your contribution, not out of your price. A 10 percent cut in price can remove a much bigger share of the money that pays your fixed costs and profit. Before you agree to any discount, calculate how many more units you must sell to end up with the same total contribution.

blocks.title: Worked example: what 10 percent off costs Ngozi
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi sells 200 packs a month at ₦1,700 with a variable cost of ₦940. A customer suggests a 10 percent 'promo' price.
steps: Current contribution = ₦1,700 minus ₦940 = ₦760 a pack. Total = 200 x ₦760 = ₦152,000.
Discounted price = ₦1,700 minus 10 percent (₦170) = ₦1,530. New contribution = ₦1,530 minus ₦940 = ₦590 a pack.
Packs needed for the same ₦152,000 = ₦152,000 divided by ₦590 = 257.6, rounded up to 258 packs.
Extra packs needed = 258 minus 200 = 58, which is 29 percent more sales, more frying and more stock.
blocks.result: A 10 percent price cut needs 29 percent more sales just to stand still. Ngozi offers a bundle instead: 5 packs for ₦8,000. Contribution on the bundle = ₦8,000 minus (5 x ₦940 = ₦4,700) = ₦3,300, or ₦660 a pack, and each sale is five packs.

blocks.title: Price cut or added value?
items: Cutting the price
Adding value
blocks.caption: Before discounting, look for a way to give more value while keeping your price.

blocks.name: business-chat
blocks.alt: Two people chatting about business on their phones
blocks.caption: Clear, friendly WhatsApp messages about value and price changes keep loyal customers on your side.

blocks.text: When a customer says 'it is too expensive'

items: Stay calm and ask what she is comparing with. Sometimes the other product is smaller or lower quality.
Restate the value: weight, freshness, finishing, delivery, after-sales adjustments.
Offer a choice instead of a cut: a smaller size, a bundle, or a simpler version at a lower price that still covers your costs.
If she still wants a lower price than your variable cost allows, thank her and let the sale go. Not every sale is a good sale.

blocks.text: When costs rise: recalculate, then decide

blocks.title: Worked example: flour goes up 20 percent
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's flour price rises from ₦15,000 to ₦18,000 for 10 kg. Everything else stays the same.
steps: Extra cost per batch = ₦18,000 minus ₦15,000 = ₦3,000. Per pack = ₦3,000 divided by 50 = ₦60.
New variable cost = ₦940 + ₦60 = ₦1,000 a pack.
If she keeps ₦1,700, contribution falls to ₦700 and break-even rises from 145 to ₦110,000 divided by ₦700 = 157.1, so 158 packs.
To keep her ₦760 contribution she needs ₦1,000 + ₦760 = ₦1,760. She rounds to ₦1,800, giving ₦800 contribution.
blocks.result: Ngozi raises her price to ₦1,800 with two weeks' notice. Her contribution is protected and break-even drops to ₦110,000 divided by ₦800 = 137.5, so 138 packs.

blocks.text: How to announce a price change

items: Give notice, for example one or two weeks, so regular customers can stock up at the old price.
Explain the reason in one honest sentence, such as higher flour and oil prices.
Remind them of the value they get: same weight, same freshness, same delivery.
Thank them, and keep the message short and warm.

blocks.title: A sample WhatsApp message
blocks.text: Good afternoon, and thank you for buying from us. Because flour and oil prices have gone up, our 250 g chin-chin will be ₦1,800 from Monday 1st. It is still freshly fried twice a week, sealed and full weight. Orders placed before Sunday stay at ₦1,700. Thank you for your support.

Wholesale customers need more notice than retail customers because they have printed their own price lists. Tell them about a month ahead if you can, and recalculate your wholesale price with the same method so that it stays well above your new variable cost.

blocks.title: Do not shrink the pack quietly
blocks.text: Reducing the weight while keeping the label and price the same is dishonest and customers notice. If you change the size, change the label and tell customers.

takeaways: Sell benefits and proof, not your costs
A discount cuts contribution, so it needs many more sales to break even on it
Bundles and added value protect your price better than cuts
When costs rise, recalculate first, then announce changes with notice and a reason

lessons.title: Monthly review, what-if planning and your next steps
objectives: Run a monthly review of prices, costs and profit
Use what-if calculations to test changes before making them
Complete the evidence for your certificate
Choose the next skill to build

blocks.text: Costs, customers and competitors keep changing, so a price that was right in January can be wrong by April. The habit that protects your profit is a short, regular review. This final lesson gives you a monthly routine, a simple what-if method for testing decisions on paper first, and the steps to complete the course.

blocks.title: Your monthly money routine
items: Week 1: prepare last month's P&L
Week 2: recheck supplier prices
Week 3: update cash forecast
Week 4: review targets and prices
blocks.caption: Spreading the work over the month means each task takes less than an hour.

blocks.text: The monthly review questions

items: Did I reach my break-even point and my profit target? By how much did I beat or miss them?
Has my gross margin moved? If it fell, which input cost rose?
Is my variable cost per unit still correct at today's supplier prices?
Did any customer pay late, and is any stock not moving?
Is my price still right for my costs and my market? Do I need to change it next month?

blocks.text: What-if planning

Before you change a price, take a bigger shop, or accept a large order, test the effect on paper. Use one simple formula: **Profit = Units sold x Contribution per unit minus Fixed costs.** Change one number at a time and see what happens to profit.

blocks.title: Worked example: Ngozi tests five scenarios
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi's base month: 250 packs at ₦1,700, variable cost ₦940 (contribution ₦760), fixed costs ₦110,000. Base profit = 250 x 760 = ₦190,000, minus ₦110,000 = ₦80,000.
steps: Variable cost up 10 percent to ₦1,034: contribution ₦666. Profit = 250 x 666 = ₦166,500 minus ₦110,000 = ₦56,500.
Sales fall 20 percent to 200 packs: profit = 200 x 760 = ₦152,000 minus ₦110,000 = ₦42,000.
Rent goes up, adding ₦20,000 to fixed costs: profit = ₦190,000 minus ₦130,000 = ₦60,000.
blocks.result: A ₦100 price rise adds ₦25,000 profit, while a 20 percent drop in sales removes ₦38,000. Ngozi now knows that protecting sales volume and price matters most, and that a 10 percent cost rise must be passed on quickly.

blocks.text: What-if for a big order

Suppose a supermarket offers Ngozi a regular order of 300 packs a month at ₦1,300, paid 30 days after delivery. Contribution = ₦1,300 minus ₦940 = ₦360 a pack, so 300 x ₦360 = ₦108,000 extra contribution a month, with no extra fixed costs if her kitchen and helper can cope. But 300 packs means 6 extra batches, so her capacity must double, and 6 x ₦47,000 = ₦282,000 of cash is tied up for a month before the first payment arrives. The order looks profitable on paper; the real questions are capacity and cash.
Signs it is time to re-price

items: Gross margin has fallen for two months in a row.
A main input such as flour, oil, fabric or packaging has risen by more than about 10 percent.
You are always sold out early, which suggests customers value the product more than your price shows.
Your fixed costs have changed, such as new rent or a new helper.

blocks.text: Where to go next

Strong costing depends on strong records, so if daily record-keeping still feels hard, take the WODDI Institute course **Simple Record-Keeping (Visual & Practical)**. To manage the money you take home, try **Savings, Spending & Budgeting Basics**. When your plan shows the business is ready to grow, **Business Registration & Compliance** and **Product Packaging & Branding** help you formalise and present it, which can also support a higher price.

blocks.title: Teach one other person
blocks.text: Explain break-even to a friend in business using her own numbers. Teaching the method is the fastest way to make sure you really understand it, and it strengthens your network.

blocks.title: Keep your estimates honest
blocks.text: Every naira figure in this course is an approximate example. Your plan is only as good as your own real, current numbers, so keep updating it.

takeaways: Review P&L, supplier prices, cash and targets every month
Profit = units x contribution per unit minus fixed costs; change one number at a time
Small price and volume changes have big effects on profit

quiz.q: Halima's fixed costs are ₦155,000 and her contribution is ₦10,600 per gown. What is her break-even point?
quiz.explain: 155,000 divided by 10,600 = 14.6, rounded up to 15 gowns.

quiz.q: Ngozi sells 200 packs at a contribution of ₦760. If she cuts her price by ₦170, contribution becomes ₦590. How many packs must she sell to earn the same total contribution?
quiz.explain: Same total = 200 x 760 = ₦152,000. 152,000 divided by 590 = 257.6, rounded up to 258 packs, 29 percent more.

quiz.q: Ngozi's variable cost rises from ₦940 to ₦1,000. What price keeps her contribution at ₦760?
quiz.explain: Price = new variable cost + desired contribution = 1,000 + 760 = ₦1,760. She may round up to ₦1,800.

quiz.q: Base month: 250 units, contribution ₦760, fixed costs ₦110,000. What is profit if sales fall 20 percent?
Halima takes a 50 percent deposit of ₦7,500 on a ₦15,000 gown whose materials cost ₦4,400. Why is this good for her cash?
options: The deposit pays for the materials before she starts
It removes the need for a P&L
quiz.explain: The deposit is larger than the materials cost, so she never funds materials from her own cash, and a cancelled order does not leave her out of pocket.

finalQuiz.q: Which cost is direct and variable for a chin-chin business?
options: Printed pouches used for each pack
finalQuiz.explain: Each pouch goes into one pack, and more packs need more pouches, so it is direct and variable.

finalQuiz.q: A fryer costing ₦96,000 is expected to last 24 months. How much should be added to monthly fixed costs for equipment wear?
A batch costs ₦36,000 and gives 40 good units. Monthly fixed costs are ₦60,000 and she sells about 150 units a month. What is the full cost per unit?
finalQuiz.explain: Variable cost per unit = 36,000 divided by 40 = ₦900. Fixed per unit = 60,000 divided by 150 = ₦400. Full cost = 900 + 400 = ₦1,300.

finalQuiz.q: A product sells for ₦2,500 with a variable cost of ₦1,500. Fixed costs are ₦120,000 a month. What is the break-even point?
finalQuiz.explain: Contribution = 2,500 minus 1,500 = ₦1,000. Break-even = 120,000 divided by 1,000 = 120 units.

finalQuiz.q: Using the same product (price ₦2,500, contribution ₦1,000, fixed costs ₦120,000), how many units give a ₦50,000 profit?
Full cost is ₦2,400 and the owner wants a 25 percent margin. What price should she charge?
finalQuiz.explain: Price = 2,400 divided by (1 minus 0.25) = 2,400 divided by 0.75 = ₦3,200. ₦3,000 would be a 25 percent markup, which is only a 20 percent margin.

finalQuiz.q: Which wholesale price should Ngozi refuse outright if her variable cost is ₦940 a pack?
finalQuiz.explain: ₦900 is below her variable cost, so every pack would lose ₦40 before any fixed costs. The others at least make some contribution.

finalQuiz.q: A month shows sales of ₦600,000, cost of goods sold of ₦330,000 and operating expenses of ₦150,000. What are the gross and net margins?
finalQuiz.explain: Gross profit = 600,000 minus 330,000 = ₦270,000, which is 45 percent. Net profit = 270,000 minus 150,000 = ₦120,000, which is 20 percent.

finalQuiz.q: A business made ₦90,000 profit but its cash fell. Which pair of events could explain this?
options: Customers paid deposits and stock fell
Large credit sales not yet paid, and a loan repayment
Equipment wear was recorded and prices rose
Sales rose and the owner took no wage
finalQuiz.explain: Credit sales count as profit before the cash arrives, and loan repayments use cash without being an expense. Both reduce cash compared with profit.

finalQuiz.q: Contribution is ₦800 a unit and the owner sells 300 units a month. She considers a 10 percent price cut that reduces contribution to ₦600. How many units must she sell to keep the same total contribution?
finalQuiz.explain: Total now = 300 x 800 = ₦240,000. 240,000 divided by 600 = 400 units, a third more sales.

finalQuiz.q: A cash forecast shows week 3 ending at minus ₦25,000. What is the best response?
options: Ignore it; the month will balance out
Act now: chase a debt, ask for deposits or delay a purchase
finalQuiz.explain: A negative week is an early warning. Acting before the week arrives, by collecting money or delaying spending, prevents a real shortage.

finalQuiz.q: Halima's gross margin dropped from 70 percent to 62 percent over two months while her price stayed the same. What should she check first?
options: Whether her lining, zip and thread prices have risen
Whether her apprentice is on time
Whether she has posted enough on WhatsApp
finalQuiz.explain: Gross margin depends on price and variable costs. With the price unchanged, a falling gross margin points to rising material costs. Rent affects net margin, not gross margin.

capstone.title: Complete Business Costing & Profit Plan
capstone.brief: Produce a one-page costing and profit plan for your real business, supported by your working pages: a complete cost calculation including all overhead categories, a break-even calculation with clear reasoning, a specific profit target with a pricing or volume plan to reach it, a projected monthly P&L and a four-week cash forecast.
steps: Record every cost for at least two weeks with dates, quantities and prices, and sort each as direct or indirect, fixed or variable.
Total monthly fixed costs, including your own wage and equipment wear, and calculate variable cost per unit from a real, counted batch or job.
Calculate full cost per unit at your average monthly volume, then set retail and wholesale prices, showing the margin each gives.
Calculate contribution per unit, break-even point in units and naira, and your margin of safety, with the working shown.
Set a monthly profit target, work back to monthly, weekly and daily sales, and check it against your capacity.
Prepare a projected monthly P&L at your planned volume and a four-week cash forecast, and note how you will fund materials.
Test three what-if scenarios and write one decision you will act on next month.
